newsitem.title: INDONESIA: Indonesia says will not change car policy.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia says will not change car policy.

text.p: Indonesia said on Tuesday it was not willing to amend its controversial national car policy and would defend the programme if Japan forwarded a complaint to the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
"If our car policy is to be brought to WTO, we will face it and solve it according to procedures," State Secretary Murdiono told reporters.
"There is no reason to change our (car) policy," he said.
Japanese Trade Minister Shunpei Tsukahara said in Tokyo on Tuesday that he wanted to discuss Indonesia's car policy when he visited the country in mid-September.
"I would like discuss the issue. I would like to deal with the issue calmly and take necessary procedures," Tsukahara told a news conference.

Japan has threatened to take Indonesia to the WTO over its national car policy which allows only PT Timor Putra Nasional to import vehicles free of tariffs and luxury taxes imposed on other car makers.
The tax breaks were given to Timor Putra in February this year on condition that it met local content requirements within three years.
Timor Putra, controlled by President Suharto's youngest son Hutomo Mandala Putra, has established a joint venture with South Korea's Kia Motors Corp to produce the cars.
The policy has also been condemned by the United States and the European Union as breaking WTO rules.
"When the government first decided on its national car, all aspects were calculated, including the possibility that the issue would be brought to the WTO," Murdiono said.
"The Industry and Trade Ministry and other ministries that are responsible for the national car policy will certainly be prepared. We should not panic in facing that problem," he said.
Meanwhile, state-owned Antara news agency quoted an executive at an automobile components maker as saying that Timor Putra was yet to reach an agreement with local component manufacturers.
Safiun, the chairman of the Indonesian Motor Component Industry Federation, said that problems on pricing had prevented any agreement being signed by Timor Putra and local manufacturers.
Under the government policy, the Timor car must contain 20 percent local content within one year of starting production and 60 percent within three years.
